transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-23
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Ortega (Redwood SE), Carlos Ruiz (BluePeak CTO), Amita Patel (BluePeak Senior ML Eng), Jon Price (BluePeak Platform Eng)
---
00:00:05 Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for making time, really appreciate it. I'm Maya, I'm the account lead for BluePeak, and Liam's gonna walk through the hosted chat onramp, streaming behavior, parameter recommendations and retry patterns.
00:00:18 Carlos Ruiz: Hi Maya, hi Liam, thanks. We're most interested in latency for live shopper assistant and also cost implications. We have an existing LLM pilot with another provider but the latency is too spiky.
00:00:30 Liam Ortega: Great, quick agenda — live demo of streaming, show how params affect output and speed, then retry/backoff playbook, quick Console tour for model routes and traces, and Optimize tips for batching/caching. We'll also cover security briefly.
00:00:45 Amita Patel: Sounds good. We care about prefix caching and how KV cache behaves across short sessions. Also curious about quantized models since we want costs down.
00:00:58 Jon Price: And VPC options — for now we want hosted but need to know path to a private VPC later.
00:01:10 Liam Ortega: Yep. Quick context check: what’s a typical prompt size and expected reply length?
00:01:16 Carlos Ruiz: Prompts are short — 40 to 120 tokens. Replies usually 60–200 tokens, but we want fast first-token latency for UI feel.
00:01:27 Liam Ortega: Understood — so we'll emphasize low first-byte latency.
---
00:01:40 Liam Ortega: Alright I'm sharing my screen — starting at the Redwood Console route creation. You can configure an endpoint with model pinning, then enable streaming which returns chunks over server-sent events.
00:01:55 Maya Chen: Note — sometimes on these recordings the product name was transcribed as "Redwood consul" but it's Console, just FYI.
00:02:05 Carlos Ruiz: Could you demo what streaming looks like client-side? We have a web socket UI that expects partial responses.
00:02:12 Liam Ortega: Sure, hitting the chat endpoint now. You'll see a small 20 token prefix and then streaming tokens every ~30ms depending on model.
00:02:25 [00:02:25] Speaker 1 (demo client): "Hello, how can I help you today?"
00:02:30 Amita Patel: I noticed sometimes tokens come in uneven bursts, is that batching on the server?
00:02:36 Liam Ortega: Good observation — continuous batching is used to increase throughput. We tune batch windows to balance latency and throughput; for low-latency UIs we use a small window and enable prefix caching. That reduces first-token latency.
00:02:50 Carlos Ruiz: When you say prefix caching, is that KV cache across sessions or per conversation? We have short-lived sessions per shopper.
00:02:58 Liam Ortega: It's per-conversation prefix caching; we also offer optional shared K V cache for specific prompt templates but that's more a Dedicated/Private feature. I might have said KV as "K V cash" earlier in another call — transcripts are messy.
00:03:12 Jon Price: If we keep sessions short, does caching help at all?
00:03:16 Liam Ortega: For repeated system prompts or instruction templates it helps even for short sessions. But for unique prompt per user, caching has less impact. The big wins are batching and quantization when throughput is high.
---
00:03:30 Liam Ortega: Now parameter matrix — key knobs are temperature, top_p, max_tokens, and presence/penalty. For controlled assistant replies with deterministic answers, keep temperature 0.0–0.2 and top_p ~0.6–0.9. Lowering temperature reduces variance and sometimes speeds up sampling slightly.
00:03:52 Amita Patel: If we do retrieval-augmented generation, would you recommend higher temperature for creative rewrite tasks?
00:03:58 Liam Ortega: Yes for rewrite/creative tasks increase to 0.7–1.0. But for slot-filling or transactional replies keep it low. We often create a param matrix per route — e.g., /shopping/assist -> temp 0.15, top_p 0.8, max_tokens 120; /creative-blurb -> temp 0.85, top_p 0.95.
00:04:20 Carlos Ruiz: Are there built-in guards for hallucinations or do we attach evals?
00:04:25 Liam Ortega: We have a quality monitoring pipeline — Redwood Optimize can track eval prompt sets and alert on regression. Also function calling and structured outputs make it easier to reduce hallucination risk.
---
00:04:38 Liam Ortega: Back to retries — hosted endpoints can return transient 5xx or 429 when capacity is tight. Best pattern: exponential backoff with jitter, idempotency tokens for non-streaming requests, and a streaming-specific fallback.
00:04:52 Maya Chen: To clarify: if a stream fails mid-response, the client should retry the request with same conversation history and an idempotency key?
00:04:59 Liam Ortega: For streaming we recommend re-requesting the missing part if the client can detect the last stable token, otherwise re-run the generation with the same inputs and use partial dedupe heuristics. We also offer server-side fallback to a cheaper model in route policy so your UI can fail to a shorter reply rather than completely time out.
00:05:20 Jon Price: That fallback feature — is it configurable per route?
00:05:24 Liam Ortega: Yes. You can set route policies: fallback model, max latency before fallback, or region fallback. It's in the Console under Route policies.
---
00:05:40 Amita Patel: We care about cost — how effective is quantization on hosted models?
00:05:45 Liam Ortega: We expose several model variants including quantized ones. For many workloads 4-bit quantization can reduce cost 2–4x with modest impact on quality. Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization based on your evals. For strict quality use the non-quantized model but try shifted traffic to quantized for A/B.
00:06:02 Carlos Ruiz: For our contract, we need SOC2 and SSO — what do you provide?
00:06:08 Maya Chen: We provide SOC2 reports for enterprise accounts, SAML SSO, RBAC roles in the Console, and KMS integration for Private deployments. For hosted, we support customer-managed keys in some regions and audit logs. I'll attach the security pack after the call.
00:06:22 Jon Price: What about data retention and deletion?
00:06:25 Liam Ortega: By default we minimize retention for hosted trials but enterprise customers can set retention windows or choose Dedicated/Private for no retention. We'll include retention options in the security doc.
---
00:06:40 Liam Ortega: Quick Console demo of a call trace — you can see token-level latency breakdown, model selection, and batching windows. This helps diagnose tail latency.
00:06:52 Carlos Ruiz: Nice, do you provide trace export to our observability (e.g., Datadog)?
00:06:56 Liam Ortega: Yes we have tracing hooks and can route traces via OTLP; we also provide raw logs and usage metrics via the Console.
---
00:07:10 Amita Patel: Could you talk about canary rollouts and A/B testing? We may want to experiment with quantized vs full model on a small percent of users.
00:07:17 Liam Ortega: Canary rollouts are first-class: you can specify traffic percentages to model variants, and Redwood will do automatic fallback if SLOs are violated. We also capture quality regressions tied to eval prompt sets so you can detect if quantized traffic hurts accuracy.
00:07:34 Carlos Ruiz: How do you recommend we run the pilot?
00:07:38 Maya Chen: Typical pilot — 2–4 week window, 1–2 routes onboarded, we run a scripted smoke with your latency targets, and we'll put a small percent of live traffic through to measure real UX. We'll provide a pilot SOW and pricing.
00:07:52 Jon Price: That sounds good. We prefer a short latency benchmark script we can run in our infra.
00:07:56 Liam Ortega: I'll share a lightweight benchmark (node/python) that runs repeated short prompts and measures first-token and 95th percentile. It includes streaming and sync modes.
---
00:08:12 [Long stretch of demo activity and screen share where Liam tweaks parameters and shows console charts — timestamps are denser here]
00:08:12 [00:08:12] Liam Ortega: (typing) Changing route settings to temp 0.12, top_p 0.8. Enabling streaming chunk size to 32 tokens.
00:08:30 [00:08:30] Amita Patel: I see that enabling a smaller chunk size increases first-byte latency but reduces tail. Is that right?
00:08:35 Liam Ortega: Actually smaller chunk size tends to decrease first-byte latency because server will flush smaller groups faster, but it can increase compute overhead. There's a tradeoff so Optimize suggests best chunk size based on your workload.
00:08:52 Carlos Ruiz: Can the Console recommend batching config?
00:08:55 Liam Ortega: Yes, Optimize provides suggestions: batch size, window, and cache settings. It correlates with cost per token and latency targets.
---
00:09:05 Jon Price: Are there any gotchas for our stack — we’re running a React front-end with long polling currently?
00:09:12 Maya Chen: For streaming we recommend SSE or websockets to avoid repeated reconnects — long polling can create latency spikes.
00:09:20 Jon Price: Good to know.
---
00:09:30 Liam Ortega: Quick Q+A — Carlos?
00:09:32 Carlos Ruiz: You mentioned idempotency tokens earlier. Do we need them for streaming?
00:09:36 Liam Ortega: Idempotency tokens are most useful for non-streaming or when you want exactly-once results. For streaming retries the client should use dedupe heuristics or re-run with same conversation context and accept overlap. We recommend using an idempotency key where possible and keep payload small.
00:09:53 Amita Patel: Can you throttle per-user to avoid abusing the rate limits?
00:09:57 Liam Ortega: Yes Console supports per-route quotas and token-level budgeting so you can limit per user or per API key.
---
00:10:10 Carlos Ruiz: Any notes about region routing? We have EU residency requirements for some customers.
00:10:15 Liam Ortega: We can pin routes to regions and enable region fallback. For regulated data we recommend Dedicated or Private with VPC and KMS for full control.
00:10:24 Maya Chen: I'll include region-specific options in the security pack.
---
00:10:30 [Mid-call recap and commitment to next steps]
00:10:30 Maya Chen: To summarize — we showed streaming behavior, parameter matrix best practices, retries/backoff playbook, Console route policies and traces, and Optimize suggestions around batching and quantization.
00:10:44 Carlos Ruiz: That was useful, thanks. Two asks: 1) security pack + SOC2, and 2) the latency benchmark script.
00:10:51 Maya Chen: Noted — we'll send both. Also we'll include a sample pilot SOW.
00:10:57 Jon Price: For timelines, if we sign pilot next week can we start within 3 business days?
00:11:03 Maya Chen: Yes, hosted onboarding is fast — usually <72 hours to get routes and test traffic.
---
00:11:10 [The call continues with some informal troubleshooting and clarifications, small cross talk and filler words retained]
00:11:10 Amita Patel: Quick thing — do the audit logs include raw inputs? We have PII concerns.
00:11:16 Liam Ortega: Audit logs can redact user content; for higher compliance we recommend Dedicated/Private and customer-managed KMS. For hosted we can limit retention and redact via policy.
00:11:30 Carlos Ruiz: Do you have references from retail customers?
00:11:35 Maya Chen: I can share anonymized case studies — I'll add those to the follow-up.
00:11:40 Amita Patel: One more — function calling: will that help us structure responses for downstream systems?
00:11:45 Liam Ortega: Yes function calls are great for structured outputs like product selection JSON so your platform can act on the response reliably.
---
00:11:55 [Wrap-up and explicit next steps recorded]
00:11:55 Maya Chen: Action items: I'll send the security pack, SOW, and pricing; Liam shares benchmark script; Amita shares prompt sets. Next meeting: pilot kickoff tentative for 2026-05-04 if contract signed.
00:12:10 Carlos Ruiz: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
00:12:15 Maya Chen: Thanks, talk soon.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings, punctuation missing and some product names come through odd (e.g., "Redwood consul"), full fidelity of timestamps intentionally coarse post-demo.
